\chapter{El inventario}
\label{ch:es-stock}
\hlchaptermodality{459}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read a shop door that is shut for the morning: why it is closed, when it opens, which part stays open, and when the usual hours come back.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.

\section[la sección]{la sección — a piece cut off}

\label{lesson:ES-C459-seccion}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{cortar} and \textbf{el almacén}. A big store has been cut into parts, and each one has a name.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la sección}
\textbf{la sección} — the section, the department.

\emph{La sección de deportes} — the sports department. \emph{¿En qué sección está?} — which part of the shop is it in? \emph{La sección de lácteos} — the dairy aisle.

Beyond shops: a section of a form, of a newspaper, of a report. Anywhere a whole has been divided and the parts labelled.

Plural \textbf{secciones}, and the accent comes off, as it does for every \emph{-ción}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: sección, parte, departamento}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what it names} & \textbf{the word} \\
\midrule
any piece of a whole & \textbf{la parte} \\
a piece somebody divided off on purpose & \textbf{la sección} \\
a unit of an organisation & \textbf{el departamento} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Una parte del libro} could be any stretch of it. \emph{Una sección del libro} is one somebody marked out and probably numbered. And a \emph{departamento} has staff.

The middle one is the useful new distinction: \emph{sección} always implies a dividing hand, which is exactly what its root says.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{secare}, \textbf{to cut} — the participle \emph{sectus} gave \emph{sectio}, a cutting.

So a \emph{sección} is a \textbf{cut piece}, and the family is full of cutting: \textbf{el insecto} is an animal cut into segments, which is what you can see on an ant.

A word to keep \emph{out} of the family, because it looks as though it belongs: \textbf{la sierra} is a saw, and also a mountain range, since a ridge of peaks looks like a saw's teeth. That picture is right, but the word is Latin \emph{serra} and has nothing to do with \emph{secare}. Two words about cutting, unrelated.

English has \textbf{section}, \textbf{sector}, \textbf{dissect}, \textbf{segment} and \textbf{insect} off the same root — and \emph{insect} is the one worth remembering, because nobody expects a bug to be named after a cut.

\emph{Cortar}, which you already have, comes from a different Latin word — \emph{curtus}, shortened — so the two are not relatives, and Spanish kept both: the everyday cutting and the bookish dividing.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item which section is it in?
  \item the sports department of the store
  \item why an insect is called that
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The section? (\textbf{La sección}.) The plural? (\textbf{Las secciones}, no accent.) What does \emph{secare} mean? (\textbf{To cut}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el inventario]{el inventario — what we found}

\label{lesson:ES-C459-inventario}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{venir} and \textbf{el almacén}. A very old verb is about to turn up in a very dull word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el inventario}
\textbf{el inventario} — the inventory, and the stocktake itself.

\begin{quote}
Cerrado por \textbf{inventario}.
\end{quote}

\emph{Hacer inventario} — to do a stocktake. \emph{Está en el inventario} — it's on the list.

That sign goes up on a shop door for a morning once or twice a year, and it is the reason this word is worth having before you need it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: cerrado por — the cause on a door}]
You have met \emph{por} plus a bare noun giving a cause on a notice. Shop doors are where it lives:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{sign} & \textbf{why they are shut} \\
\midrule
\emph{cerrado por inventario} & stocktaking \\
\emph{cerrado por obras} & building work \\
\emph{cerrado por vacaciones} & holidays \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

No article, no verb, no explanation. The frame is \emph{cerrado por} + the reason, and a Spanish reader takes the whole thing in at a glance from across a street — which is what a sign is for.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{invenire}: \textbf{in-} plus \textbf{venire}, \textbf{to come} — so \emph{to come upon}, and from there \textbf{to find}.

An \emph{inventario} is therefore a \textbf{list of what was found}, which is exactly what a stocktake produces: somebody walks the shelves and writes down what is actually there, as opposed to what the records claim.

The same \emph{invenire} gave \textbf{inventar}, to invent — and that is the same idea seen from the other side. To invent something is to \emph{come upon} it. Spanish and English both treat discovery and invention as one act, and the word for a warehouse list is the proof.

\emph{Venir} is underneath all of it, and you have had it since the early lessons.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item closed for stocktaking
  \item it's not on the list
  \item what \emph{invenire} literally means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The stocktake? (\textbf{El inventario}.) Closed for it? (\textbf{Cerrado por inventario}.) Which verb is inside it? (\textbf{Venir} — to come upon, to find.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[habitual]{habitual — the way it usually is}

\label{lesson:ES-C459-habitual}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{he hablado} and \textbf{siempre}. The \emph{he} in the first is about to turn up in an adjective.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: habitual}
\textbf{habitual} — usual, regular, customary.

\emph{El horario habitual} — the usual hours. \emph{Nuestro proveedor habitual} — our regular supplier. \emph{Lo habitual es avisar} — the usual thing is to let people know.

\textbf{Habitualmente} is the adverb, and \textbf{el cliente habitual} is a regular. The opposite is \emph{poco habitual} — unusual — rather than any single word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: habitual, normal, siempre}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you mean} & \textbf{the word} \\
\midrule
this is the pattern, by habit & \textbf{habitual} \\
this is ordinary, not strange & \textbf{normal} \\
without exception & \textbf{siempre} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{El horario habitual} is the one they usually keep — and this week they may not. \emph{Es normal} means nobody should be surprised. \emph{Siempre abren a las nueve} allows no exceptions at all.

So \emph{habitual} sits between the other two: stronger than \textquotedblleft{}not strange\textquotedblright{}, weaker than \textquotedblleft{}always\textquotedblright{}. A notice using it is telling you what to expect while leaving itself room.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{habēre}, \textbf{to have, to hold} — by way of \emph{habitus}, \textquotedblleft{}the way one holds oneself\textquotedblright{}.

You own that verb already: \emph{habēre} is the \textbf{haber} of \emph{he hablado}, worn down by centuries of use into an auxiliary so small it barely looks like a word. Set the two side by side and the two roads are visible again:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{worn down by speech} & \textbf{lifted from the page} \\
\midrule
\textbf{he} hablado & \textbf{habit}ual \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A habit is something you \emph{hold}, which is why English says you \textbf{have} a habit rather than doing one. And \emph{el hábito} in Spanish is both a habit and a monk's robe — the clothing you hold yourself in, from the same \emph{habitus}.

The \textbf{h} is silent, as it is anywhere in Spanish that it stands on its own.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the usual hours
  \item our regular supplier
  \item which of \emph{habitual} and \emph{siempre} allows an exception
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Usual? (\textbf{Habitual}.) What does \emph{habēre} mean? (\textbf{To have, to hold}.) Which everyday word is it worn down into? (\textbf{Haber} — \emph{he hablado}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(la sección, el inventario, habitual)]{(la sección, el inventario, habitual) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R459-repaso-stock}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all three: \emph{the section}, \emph{the stocktake}, \emph{usual}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two everyday verbs, hidden in office words}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{office word} & \textbf{the everyday verb inside it} \\
\midrule
el \textbf{invent}ario & \textbf{venir} — \emph{in-venire}, to come upon \\
\textbf{habit}ual & \textbf{haber} — \emph{habēre}, to hold \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both verbs are among the first things anybody learns in Spanish, and both are so worn down that nothing on the surface connects them to these words. An inventory is \textbf{a list of what was found}; something habitual is \textbf{a thing held on to}.

This is what happens when a language takes the same Latin word twice. The spoken copy shrinks until it is almost nothing — \emph{he}, \emph{vengo} — while the written copy keeps its whole Latin shape.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the notice frames, collected}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{frame} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
\emph{cerrado por} + bare noun & \emph{cerrado por inventario} \\
\emph{fuera de} + bare noun & \emph{fuera de plazo} \\
\emph{por} + bare noun, as a cause & \emph{por obras} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

No article after any of them. Spanish signs run on these three shapes, and once you can see the frame you can read a notice you have never met by filling in one word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item closed for stocktaking
  \item the usual hours in the sports section
  \item which verb is inside \emph{inventario}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(cerrado por inventario) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C459-sintesis-stock}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el inventario} and \textbf{habitual}. The door below uses one to excuse breaking the other.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A sheet taped to a shop door. Read it, then answer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{CERRADO POR INVENTARIO}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Solo esta mañana. Abrimos a las 16:00.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
El \textbf{horario habitual} se recupera mañana.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
La \textbf{sección} de deportes permanece abierta por la puerta lateral.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item how long the shop is shut, and when it opens
  \item what is open anyway, and how to get in
  \item when things go back to normal
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{El horario habitual se recupera mañana} is the line worth taking apart. \emph{Habitual} rather than \emph{normal}, because the shop is saying \emph{this is the pattern we keep}, not \emph{this is not strange}. And \emph{se recupera} rather than \emph{recuperamos}: the timetable comes back by itself, nobody is thanked for it.

\textbf{Permanece abierta} agrees with \emph{la sección}, feminine — a small check that catches people out, because \emph{deportes} is masculine and plural and sits right next to the verb. Spanish agrees with the head noun, not with the nearest one.

And the heading is the frame you now know: \emph{cerrado por} plus a bare noun. A reader takes it in from the pavement without reading the rest.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four lines for a shop door: say you are closed for stocktaking, say when you reopen, say the usual hours come back tomorrow, and say which section stays open.

Then check yourself: did you use the \emph{cerrado por} frame with no article, and did the adjective agree with \emph{la sección} rather than with \emph{deportes}?
\end{tcolorbox}
